newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: IAEA says Iraq still likely hiding nuclear data.
newsitem.headline: IAEA says Iraq still likely hiding nuclear data.

text.p: Iraq is probably still concealing significant documents about its clandestine nuclear weapons programme and may be hiding material and equipment, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency said on Thursday.

"While recognising that a very extensive documentation of the Iraqi nuclear programme has been assembled ... can we be sure that nothing further is withheld? The answer is no," IAEA Director-General Hans Blix told the Security Council.

Blix, whose agency is responsible for making sure Iraq's nuclear weapons programme has been dismantled, said modern technology allowed easy transfer of written records into magnetic, optic, photographic or electronic media that did not require much space and could be quickly hidden or removed.

"We see no evidence of any remaining nuclear weapons production capacity -- with the exception of one important element: knowledge and know-how, which are indestructible," he said at a closed-door briefing.

According to Blix's briefing paper, which later became available, when he told a senior Iraqi official in June that the IAEA believed the "well-organised Iraqi government still retained a full record of its past nuclear programme, he indignantly denied this."

"However, such denials do not carry any weight. We cannot and do not act on the basis of trust. We still think it is probable that significant documentation is concealed and withheld. Some material and equipment could also be hidden and components of equipment could be moved around, escaping even very thorough and rigorous monitoring."

Blix said his agency's ongoing monitoring and verification (OMV) system in Iraq was "the major tool at hand to deter the reconstitution by Iraq of a nuclear weapon oriented programme and to provide early warning in case the nuclear knowledge and know-how were to turn to proscribed activities."

But he said the IAEA and the U.N. Special Commission in charge of scrapping Iraq's chemical, biological and ballistic weapons programmes were in serious financial straits and would "have to implement a contingency plan for a gradual closure of operations" unless they get more funds in the next few weeks.
This envisaged withdrawing the IAEA nuclear monitoring group from Iraq in the first week of January and the closing down of its action team operations by the end of February.
"Needless to say I hope we shall not have to put this plan into operation," he added.
